title: Truck Driver
oneLiner: The highway middle is going. The first mile, the last mile and the paperwork are not.
summary: Trucking is the job where the automation story has been ten years away for fifteen years, and the reason is instructive: the driving was the easy part. Long-haul motorway driving is genuinely being automated — it is repetitive, mapped, and commercially valuable enough to justify the investment. Driverless freight corridors are operating commercially in parts of the US. What resists is everything at the ends of the route: urban delivery, loading and securing, the customer who signs, the awkward yard, the breakdown, the load that shifts. The likely shape is not mass unemployment but a split, with hub-to-hub motorway sections automated and human drivers doing the complicated ends. Regulation, insurance and liability move slowly, and each buys the profession years.

tasks.name: Motorway long-haul driving
tasks.note: The most automatable segment: predictable, mapped, high value. Driverless freight corridors are already in commercial operation.

tasks.name: Route planning & dispatch
tasks.note: Optimised by software including traffic, hours-of-service rules and fuel. Dispatch roles thinned out first.

tasks.name: Logging & compliance paperwork
tasks.note: Electronic logging is mandatory and automatic in most markets.

tasks.name: Yard manoeuvring & docking
tasks.note: Automated in controlled private yards. Tight, unmapped, real-world docks are a different problem entirely.

tasks.name: Urban & last-mile delivery
tasks.note: Unpredictable streets, double-parked cars, gestures from a person waving you back. Cost per mile is highest exactly where automation is hardest.

tasks.name: Loading and securing freight
tasks.note: Straps, pallets, tail lifts, a load that shifted in transit. Physical work with legal safety consequences.

tasks.name: Handling breakdowns, accidents and refusals
tasks.note: Blown tyre on a hard shoulder, a customer refusing delivery, a road closed with no diversion. The long tail is where drivers earn their pay.

tasks.name: Customer contact & handover
tasks.note: Someone signs for the goods, checks the condition and answers for what arrived.

whatSurvives: Both ends of the route — everything that is not a mapped motorway in good weather.
adaptPrompt:
You are my logistics and business assistant. I drive; you handle the paperwork and the numbers that decide whether a load is worth taking.

For loads and rates — this is where owner-operators lose money:
1. Given a load offer (origin, destination, rate, weight, deadhead miles), calculate my real cost per mile: fuel at current price and my truck's mpg, tolls, maintenance reserve, insurance, and my time. Then tell me the actual profit, not the gross.
2. Compare it to what I should be getting on that lane and tell me plainly whether to take it, negotiate it or decline it.
3. Flag the hidden costs: detention risk, a delivery window I cannot make legally, an area where I will sit empty afterwards.

For operations:
4. Plan the route against my hours-of-service: where my breaks land, where I will legally park for the night, and where the timing is tight.
5. Explain the specific permits, restrictions and rules for the states or countries I am crossing.
6. Draft the professional message when something goes wrong — a delay, damage, a refused delivery — that protects my position and stays civil.

For the business:
7. Track my numbers by month and tell me which lanes and which brokers actually make me money, and which I keep running out of habit.

Rules: never tell me to run over my legal hours or push through fatigue. If a load only works by breaking the rules, say the load does not work. Show your arithmetic on every rate calculation so I can check it at a truck stop.
